newsitem.title: USA: Calif. power marketers take aim at big customers.
newsitem.headline: Calif. power marketers take aim at big customers.

text.p: California's big electricity users are poised to ramp up their efforts to secure cheaper power following the state's decision to allow all buyers to choose from an array of suppliers starting Jan 1, industry sources said.
"Certainly marketers and others will pick up the pace now," said Bobby Campo, head of Portland General Electric Co's California marketing office.

Behind the rush is California Public Utilities Commission's (CPUC's) decision last week to abandon plans to gradually phase-in retail competition, instead giving everyone the right to choose their own power provider from January 1.
But initial marketing efforts have been, and are expected to remain, directed at large industrial and commercial users.
"Residential and small business customers know they will get a 10 percent rate reduction. There is not much incentive for them to jump right away," Campo noted.

Under California legislation, smaller utility customers are guaranteed the 10 percent rate cut through January 1, 2002. It will be financed by special bonds backed by revenue from what are called "competitive transition charges" appended to electricity bills over the same four-year period.
The yet-to-be-determined charges will be used to pay down the investor-owned utilities' stranded costs, which are estimated to total as much as $28 billion.
Stranded costs include assets such as nuclear power plants that were built during the era of strict utility regulation and are not likely to be profitable in a competitive market.

The state's traditional monopoly utilities, Edison International's, Southern California Edison Co, PG&E Corp's Pacific Gas & Electric Co and Enova Corp's San Diego Gas & Electric Co, will continue to deliver electricity over a regulated network of power lines.
But the cost of those distribution services also will not be outlined by the CPUC until at least June.
Lots of other details, including operating criteria for a centralized power exchange pool and independent transmission system operator, are also still in the formative stages.

"Only California could create new regulatory agencies in the process of deregulating," said Robert McCullough at Oregon-based McCullough Research, a consulting firm specializing in power transactions.
"The real issue is whether they are going to have these incredibily complex, bureaucratic systems in place by January," he noted.
McCullough said some clients looking to sell power into California at the retail level estimate the new administrative requirements will add between two and 24 hours to power scheduling requirements.

Although such risk factors are likely to limit the number of consumers looking to immediately switch from their current monopoly utility provider, sources say some companies are seeking to aggregate smaller loads and offer lower prices.
This is especially apparent at the local government level.
Cities like Palm Springs and South San Francisco have already acted to buy bulk power from outside providers as of next year.
In addition, several of the state's large commercial and industrial end-users, as well as other government entities, have opened tenders for long-term electricity supplies.
Earlier this month, the San Francisco Building Owners and Managers Association asked for proposals to supply 1,200 megawatts (MW) of power to its members from next January.
The association represents 250 commercial buildings in the city, including landmarks like the TransAmerica and BankAmerica headquarters, which are currently served by PG&E.

The Association of California Water Agencies and the Association of Bay Area Governments have also issued requests proposals to supply power to their members next year, as has the University of California, which has a vast campus network.
But bids to supply buyers over widespread locations are complicated by the fact that they are served by both investor-owned and municipal utilities, sources noted.
California's electricity restructuring legislation does not require municipal utilities, such as the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power, to open their service territories to competition.
